title: Nail Gun Safety
summary: Understanding the trigger is the key to nail gun safety. Sequential triggers cut injuries; contact (bump) triggers cause about twice as many. This talk covers trigger choice, muzzle control, and disconnecting air.
talking_points: Use a nail gun with a full sequential trigger: press the nose against the workpiece first, then pull the trigger. Contact (bump) triggers cause about twice as many injuries and do not save time overall.
Keep the nail gun pointed away from your body and other people, especially with the air connected.
Disconnect the compressed air when you leave the gun unattended, move up or down a ladder or stairs, hand it to a coworker, clear a jam, or do maintenance.
Use a hammer when you cannot reach the work while holding the gun in your dominant hand. When toe-nailing, do not force the gun flush against the workpiece.
Wear Z87+ safety glasses, hearing protection, and steel-toe footwear. Get training on safe nail gun use.
Never use a gun with a broken or modified trigger or contact spring. Never hold the trigger down unless you mean to fire, and never fire until the nose is firmly on the workpiece.
site_hazards_to_check: Contact/bump triggers in use where sequential triggers should be used
Broken, modified, or taped triggers or workpiece contact springs
Air left connected while clearing jams, climbing, or passing the tool
Workers without Z87+ glasses, hearing protection, or steel-toe boots
Crew crowded close together during nailing, risking nails driven through or ricocheting off material
discussion_questions: What trigger type is on the guns we are using, and is it right for this work?
When exactly do you disconnect the air line?
Why is holding the trigger down while carrying the gun dangerous?
